content: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has significantly reduced both mortality and morbidity associated with HIV, transforming it into a chronic condition that requires lifelong management. However, individuals living with HIV frequently experience coinfections and comorbidities, including physical and mental health disorders as well as substance use disorders. Comprehensive HIV care encompasses a range of interventions, including combination HIV prevention strategies, promotion of general health and well-being, maintenance of quality of life, and the prevention and management of coinfections and comorbidities. This care also includes antiretroviral therapy (ART), regular screening, and prophylactic measures. Children and adolescents are advised to engage in at least 60 minutes of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity daily, primarily aerobic, spread across the week. Additionally, vigorous-intensity aerobic activities and muscleand bone-strengthening exercises should be performed at least three days per week. Limiting sedentary behavior, particularly recreational screen time, is also strongly recommended. For adults aged 18–64 years and older adults aged 65 years and above, regular physical activity is essential. Adults should aim for 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity, or an equivalent combination of both intensities weekly to achieve substantial health benefits. Muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups should be performed on two or more days per week. Older adults are further encouraged to include multicomponent physical activities emphasizing functional balance and strength training at least three days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. Globally, insufficient physical activity is a significant concern, with one in four adults and four out of five adolescents not meeting recommended activity levels. Increased physical activity could prevent 4–5 million deaths annually. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed evidence-based guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behavior, which governments can integrate into national health policies. These guidelines highlight the health benefits of physical activity, including reduced all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, incident hypertension, site-specific cancers, type 2 diabetes, improved mental health, cognitive function, and sleep quality. Countries are encouraged to establish a comprehensive package of general HIV care interventions alongside ART to reduce HIV transmission, prevent illness, and improve the quality of life for people living with HIV. This package includes psychosocial counseling, partner notification, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, tuberculosis (TB) screening and preventive therapy, prevention of fungal infections, reproductive health support, cervical cancer screening, malaria prevention, vaccinations, nutrition, family planning, prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission, needle and syringe programs, and water sanitation and hygiene measures. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, a fixed-dose combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, is a cost-effective and widely available intervention to reduce HIV-related morbidity and mortality. It is recommended for adults, including pregnant women, with advanced HIV disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) or CD4 cell counts ≤350 cells/mm³. In settings with high prevalence of malaria or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be initiated regardless of CD4 count or clinical stage. It may be discontinued in clinically stable individuals on ART with evidence of immune recovery and viral suppression, except in high-prevalence settings where continuation is advised. For children and adolescents with HIV, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended regardless of clinical or immune status, with priority given to children under five years of age and those with advanced HIV disease or low CD4 counts. In high-prevalence settings, prophylaxis should continue into adulthood, irrespective of ART status. For HIV-exposed infants, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should begin at 4–6 weeks of age and continue until HIV infection is excluded through appropriate testing. The benefits of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis extend beyond preventing opportunistic infections like Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and toxoplasmosis. It also reduces the risk of malaria, severe bacterial infections, and hospitalization. Observational studies and randomized trials support its effectiveness in reducing mortality and morbidity among people living with HIV, particularly in resource-limited settings with high prevalence of malaria and bacterial infections. Continuation of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in such settings simplifies HIV management and improves access to this life-saving intervention.
